clue.text: Competitor withdrawing from race course after midday loses nothing

indicators.note: 'after' puts the course word behind the midday word in the answer
something that loses a thing has it taken away, so a letter drops out of the combined word

blocks.note: midday is noon
a starter is the first course of a meal
nothing is zero, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A runner pulls out of a race meeting at the course just after noon, empty-handed.
explanation.walkthrough: NOON plus STARTER loses one O to give NON-STARTER. 'Race course' reads as one thing, but 'course' is the meal course.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-starter is literally an entrant scratched before a race begins, hence one withdrawing from it.

clue.text: Tastier sorbet, say, eaten by empty neighbour

indicators.note: an empty word has had its inside removed, leaving only its first and last letters
something eaten by another ends up inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the outside letters of neighbour
sorbet is an example of an ice, the 'say' marking it as an example

explanation.surface: Someone finds a sorbet more delicious when a hungry neighbour wolfs it down.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicer can mean more pleasant to eat, so tastier works as a comparative synonym for food.

clue.text: Malice admitted by gymnast in Essex

blocks.note: the letters run across all three words

explanation.walkthrough: Essex is a county east of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Malice is the wish to hurt others, which is spiteful unkindness, the same quality as nastiness.

clue.text: Drunk turned up and caught a Puccini work

taken as written

explanation.surface: A drunk staggers into the opera house and gets caught watching Puccini.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosca is one of the Italian composer's most famous operas, first staged in Rome in 1900.

clue.text: Friend of Harry’s working under Rex

explanation.walkthrough: Harry is Harry Potter, and 'Rex' looks like a dog's name or a person but is the king.
explanation.definitionFit: Ron Weasley is Harry Potter's best friend in the J. K. Rowling novels.

clue.text: Old policeman with energy to become really angry

clue.text: Where roofers work for free

explanation.definitionFit: A drink offered by the bar costs the customer nothing, while roofers literally stand atop buildings.

clue.text: Thieves — or where they might end up

blocks.note: first meaning, as a verb: steals
second meaning: police stations or prisons, in British slang

explanation.walkthrough: 'Thieves' reads as a plural noun, but it is the verb meaning steals. In British slang the nick is a police station or jail.
explanation.definitionFit: To nick is informal British for stealing, and a criminal arrested is taken to the nick.

clue.text: Following tabloid, see blemish on the face of a star

definitions.text: blemish on the face of a star

indicators.note: the seeing word comes following the newspaper, so it is placed after it

blocks.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
to spot is to see

explanation.surface: A tabloid zooms in on a pimple on a celebrity's face.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'star' sounds like a celebrity caught by the paparazzi; it is the Sun itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunspots are dark patches on the visible surface of our nearest star, like marks on a face.

clue.text: Utterly hot, moving about

explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving about' looks like one phrase, but 'about' is a separate piece of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Thoroughly and utterly both mean completely, through and through, as adverbs of degree.

clue.text: DJ cross during day before party
